claim: C. elegans has risen to the status of a top model organism for biological research in the last fifty years.
source: The roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans has risen to the status of a top model organism for biological research in the last fifty years.
evidence: This is a general statement about the status of C. elegans in biological research, representing established knowledge in the scientific community.

claim: C. elegans is one of the simplest and easiest organisms to handle among laboratory animals.
source: Among laboratory animals, this tiny nematode is one of the simplest and easiest organisms to handle.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about C. elegans as a laboratory organism.

claim: C. elegans has a boom-and-bust lifestyle.
source: Like other model organisms, C. elegans has a boom-and-bust lifestyle.
evidence: This is supported by observational data and inference from population studies described in the manuscript.

claim: C. elegans feasts on ephemeral bacterial blooms in decomposing fruits and stems.
source: It feasts on ephemeral bacterial blooms in decomposing fruits and stems.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from field studies.

claim: After resource depletion, C. elegans young larvae enter a migratory diapause stage called the dauer.
source: After resource depletion, its young larvae enter a migratory diapause stage, called the dauer.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans developmental biology.

claim: Snails, slugs and isopods are migration vectors associated with C. elegans.
source: Organisms known to be associated with C. elegans include migration vectors (such as snails, slugs and isopods) and pathogens (such as microsporidia, fungi, bacteria and viruses).
evidence: This is supported by observational data and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Microsporidia, fungi, bacteria and viruses are pathogens associated with C. elegans.
source: Organisms known to be associated with C. elegans include migration vectors (such as snails, slugs and isopods) and pathogens (such as microsporidia, fungi, bacteria and viruses).
evidence: This is supported by observational data and citations in the manuscript.

claim: Emile Maupas conducted initial work on C. elegans mode of reproduction.
source: After initial work by Emile Maupas (Maupas, 1900) and Victor Nigon (Nigon, 1949; Nigon et al., 1960) on its mode of reproduction, meiosis and development, experiments by Sydney Brenner and collaborators in the 1960s and 1970s raised C. elegans to the status of a premier model organism.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maupas, 1900.

claim: Victor Nigon conducted work on C. elegans mode of reproduction, meiosis and development.
source: After initial work by Emile Maupas (Maupas, 1900) and Victor Nigon (Nigon, 1949; Nigon et al., 1960) on its mode of reproduction, meiosis and development, experiments by Sydney Brenner and collaborators in the 1960s and 1970s raised C. elegans to the status of a premier model organism.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nigon, 1949 and Nigon et al., 1960.

claim: Experiments by Sydney Brenner and collaborators in the 1960s and 1970s raised C. elegans to the status of a premier model organism.
source: After initial work by Emile Maupas (Maupas, 1900) and Victor Nigon (Nigon, 1949; Nigon et al., 1960) on its mode of reproduction, meiosis and development, experiments by Sydney Brenner and collaborators in the 1960s and 1970s raised C. elegans to the status of a premier model organism.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the history of C. elegans research.

claim: The C. elegans genome was the first to be sequenced for a multicellular organism.
source: Besides its genome, the first to be sequenced for a multicellular organism (The C. elegans Sequencing Consortium, 1998), an extensive body of knowledge is now available on the molecular, cellular, developmental and behavioral biology (The C. elegans Research Community) of this organism.
evidence: This is supported by citation to The C. elegans Sequencing Consortium, 1998.

claim: Key discoveries including the molecular mechanisms of apoptosis have been made by studying C. elegans.
source: A number of key discoveries have been made by studying C. elegans, including the molecular mechanisms of apoptosis (Conradt and Xue, 2005) and gene silencing by small RNAs (Grishok, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Conradt and Xue, 2005.

claim: Gene silencing by small RNAs was discovered by studying C. elegans.
source: A number of key discoveries have been made by studying C. elegans, including the molecular mechanisms of apoptosis (Conradt and Xue, 2005) and gene silencing by small RNAs (Grishok, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Grishok, 2013.

claim: The C. elegans reference strain N2 was originally isolated in Bristol, England.
source: This strain, originally isolated in Bristol, England, was cultured in the laboratory for many years before it was first frozen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the origin of the N2 strain.

claim: The N2 strain was cultured in the laboratory for many years before it was first frozen.
source: This strain, originally isolated in Bristol, England, was cultured in the laboratory for many years before it was first frozen.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the history of the N2 strain.

claim: The laboratory environment of N2 consisted of agar plates seeded with Escherichia coli as a food source.
source: Its laboratory environment consisted of agar plates seeded with Escherichia coli as a food source.
evidence: This is established knowledge about laboratory culture conditions.

claim: E. coli was used as food for C. elegans because it was already available in many laboratories as another model organism, not because it was originally associated with wild C. elegans.
source: E. coli was used because, as another model organism, it was already available in many laboratories—not because it was originally associated with wild C. elegans.
evidence: This is an inference about the historical reasons for using E. coli.

claim: Several mutations appeared and were fixed in the N2 lineage by comparing it with an independent subculture from the same wild Bristol isolate maintained in liquid axenic culture.
source: An independent subculture from the same wild Bristol isolate was maintained in liquid axenic culture, and by comparing both strains, we now know of several mutations that appeared and were fixed in the N2 lineage, some of which appear adaptive in the agar plate environment.
evidence: This is supported by data from comparative studies.

claim: Some mutations in the N2 lineage appear adaptive in the agar plate environment.
source: An independent subculture from the same wild Bristol isolate was maintained in liquid axenic culture, and by comparing both strains, we now know of several mutations that appeared and were fixed in the N2 lineage, some of which appear adaptive in the agar plate environment.
evidence: This is supported by inference from comparative data.

claim: C. elegans N2 has been modified by domestication.
source: Like other model organisms, C. elegans N2 has thus been modified by domestication.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed mutations and their effects.

claim: For a century, the only information available on the natural history of C. elegans was that it could be found in compost heaps and in rich humus.
source: For a century, the only information available on the natural history of C. elegans was that it could be found in compost heaps and in rich humus (Hodgkin and Doniach, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hodgkin and Doniach, 1997.

claim: From 2000 onward, researchers embarked on an extensive sampling of wild C. elegans populations.
source: From 2000 onward, this began to change when researchers embarked on an extensive sampling of wild C. elegans populations.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of C. elegans research.

claim: Researchers were motivated to develop C. elegans into a model organism for evolutionary biology and ecology research.
source: Their efforts were motivated by wanting to develop C. elegans into a model organism for evolutionary biology and ecology research, which could also leverage the tools and knowledge already acquired for this species.
evidence: This is a statement about the motivations of researchers.

claim: C. elegans is found worldwide, predominantly in humid temperate areas.
source: C. elegans is found worldwide, predominantly in humid temperate areas (Figures 1 and 2A-D) (Kiontke et al., 2011; Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and figures showing distribution.

claim: C. elegans was originally isolated in rich soil or compost.
source: This species was originally isolated in rich soil or compost (Hodgkin and Doniach, 1997), where it is mostly found in a non-feeding stage called the dauer (Barrière and Félix, 2005a, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hodgkin and Doniach, 1997.

claim: In rich soil or compost, C. elegans is mostly found in a non-feeding stage called the dauer.
source: This species was originally isolated in rich soil or compost (Hodgkin and Doniach, 1997), where it is mostly found in a non-feeding stage called the dauer (Barrière and Félix, 2005a, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Barrière and Félix, 2005a, 2007.

claim: Feeding and reproducing stages of C. elegans have been found in decomposing plant material, such as fruits and thick herbaceous stems.
source: More recently, feeding and reproducing stages of C. elegans have been found in decomposing plant material, such as fruits and thick herbaceous stems (Figure 2E–G) (Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation and figures.

claim: Rotting substrates in their late stages of decomposition provide abundant bacterial food for C. elegans.
source: These rotting substrates in their late stages of decomposition provide abundant bacterial food for the nematode.
evidence: This is an inference from observational data.

claim: C. elegans is partially associated with human activity (cultivated fruits and stems, compost).
source: Like other model organisms, C. elegans is thus partially associated with human activity (cultivated fruits and stems, compost), but the species is also commonly found on stems and fruits in wilder settings, such as woods (Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation and observational data.

claim: C. elegans is commonly found on stems and fruits in wilder settings, such as woods.
source: Like other model organisms, C. elegans is thus partially associated with human activity (cultivated fruits and stems, compost), but the species is also commonly found on stems and fruits in wilder settings, such as woods (Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Félix and Duveau, 2012.

claim: If well fed, newly hatched C. elegans individuals pass through four larval stages (L1, L2, L3, L4) and reach the adult stage after 3 days.
source: If well fed, newly hatched individuals pass through four larval stages (L1, L2, L3, L4) and reach the adult stage after 3 days.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Under stressful conditions (such as crowding, limited food supply, and heat stress), C. elegans individuals can shift during the L1 stage to an alternative developmental route and enter a predauer stage (L2d), followed by the non-feeding diapause stage called dauer.
source: Under stressful conditions (such as crowding, limited food supply, and heat stress), individuals can shift during the L1 stage to an alternative developmental route and enter a predauer stage (L2d), followed by the non-feeding diapause stage called dauer (an alternative L3 stage) (Figure 3).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: Dauer larvae are resistant to various stresses and can survive for several months without food.
source: Dauer larvae are resistant to various stresses and can survive for several months without food.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dauer physiology.

claim: Upon their return to more favorable conditions, dauer larvae feed again and resume development.
source: Upon their return to more favorable conditions, dauer larvae feed again and resume development.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dauer development.

claim: Population demographic surveys at the local scale in orchards and woods indicate that C. elegans has a boom-and-bust lifestyle.
source: Population demographic surveys at the local scale in orchards and woods indicate that C. elegans has a boom-and-bust lifestyle (Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Félix and Duveau, 2012.

claim: C. elegans metapopulations evolve in a fluctuating environment where optimal habitats are randomly distributed in space and time.
source: C. elegans metapopulations evolve in a fluctuating environment where optimal habitats are randomly distributed in space and time (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference from observational data and population studies.

claim: A cycle of colonization of a food source likely begins when one to several dauer larvae discover a fruit or stem, exit the dauer stage and seed a growing population of up to 10^4 feeding nematodes at different life-cycle stages.
source: A cycle of colonization of a food source likely begins when one to several dauer larvae discover a fruit or stem, exit the dauer stage and seed a growing population of up to 104 feeding nematodes at different life-cycle stages (Figure 3).
evidence: This is an inference from observational data.

claim: Some moderate-sized C. elegans populations found in rotting fruits and stems do not contain any dauer larvae.
source: Some moderate-sized populations found in rotting fruits and stems do not contain any dauer larvae, but larger ones always include only adults, L1, L2d and dauers (Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation and observational data.

claim: Larger C. elegans populations always include only adults, L1, L2d and dauers.
source: Some moderate-sized populations found in rotting fruits and stems do not contain any dauer larvae, but larger ones always include only adults, L1, L2d and dauers (Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation and observational data.

claim: As a food source runs low, dauers may leave it to explore the neighboring environment for new islands of resources.
source: As a food source runs low, dauers may leave it to explore the neighboring environment for new islands of resources.
evidence: This is an inference from observational data and knowledge of dauer behavior.

claim: Dauer larvae display active locomotion and a specific behavior called nictation, where they stand on their tail and wave their body in the air.
source: Dauer larvae display active locomotion and a specific behavior called nictation, where they stand on their tail and wave their body in the air.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dauer behavior.

claim: Dauers may congregate to form a column and nictate as a group.
source: Remarkably, dauers may also congregate to form a column and nictate as a group (Félix and Duveau, 2012) (see the video; http://www.wormatlas.org/dauer/behavior/Images/DBehaviorVID4.mov).
evidence: This is supported by citation and video evidence.

claim: Dauer behaviors are thought to help dauers to find passing invertebrate hosts that they can use for their dispersal, such as isopods, snails and slugs.
source: These behaviors are thought to help dauers to find passing invertebrate hosts that they can use for their dispersal, such as isopods, snails and slugs.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed behaviors.

claim: Dauer physiology and behavior suggest that this developmental stage plays a key role in C. elegans' stress resistance, long-distance dispersal, and possibly its overwintering capacity.
source: Together, dauer physiology and behavior suggest that this developmental stage plays a key role in C. elegans' stress resistance, long-distance dispersal, and possibly its overwintering capacity.
evidence: This is an inference from observed physiology and behavior.

claim: In surveys performed in France and Germany, C. elegans populations in rotting fruits typically peak in the fall, with proliferation possible in spring through to early winter.
source: Over the year, in surveys performed in France and Germany, C. elegans populations in rotting fruits typically peak in the fall, with proliferation possible in spring through to early winter (Félix and Duveau, 2012; Petersen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to field studies.

claim: The seasonal dynamic of C. elegans is consistent with that observed in a semi-natural habitat, such as a compost heap, where C. elegans population size varies over the year, from a dense population in autumn to one that declines and undergoes bottlenecks in winter.
source: This seasonal dynamic is consistent with that observed in a semi-natural habitat, such as a compost heap, where C. elegans population size varies over the year, from a dense population in autumn to one that declines and undergoes bottlenecks in winter (Figure 4B) (Barrière and Félix, 2007; Petersen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and figure showing population dynamics.

claim: Bottlenecks in C. elegans populations can lead to local extinctions.
source: These bottlenecks can lead to local extinctions.
evidence: This is an inference from population data.

claim: When local extinction occurs, a new genotype may colonize the compost heap when favorable conditions return.
source: Where this happens, a new genotype may colonize the compost heap when favorable conditions return (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At the global scale, C. elegans genetic diversity is low and displays little geographical structure.
source: At the global scale, C. elegans genetic diversity is low and displays little geographical structure, which must be due to long-distance migration, perhaps aided by larger hosts, such as birds, rodents or humans (see Box 1).
evidence: This is supported by genetic data and inference about migration.

claim: Low geographical structure in C. elegans genetic diversity must be due to long-distance migration, perhaps aided by larger hosts, such as birds, rodents or humans.
source: At the global scale, C. elegans genetic diversity is low and displays little geographical structure, which must be due to long-distance migration, perhaps aided by larger hosts, such as birds, rodents or humans (see Box 1).
evidence: This is speculation based on genetic patterns.

claim: At a local scale, founder effects have a huge impact on C. elegans genetic diversity, with low diversity in a given sample contrasting with high molecular diversity but weak haplotype diversity at the scale of a square kilometer.
source: In contrast, at a local scale, founder effects have a huge impact, with low diversity in a given sample contrasting with high molecular diversity but weak haplotype diversity at the scale of a square kilometer (Barrière and Félix, 2005a; Haber et al., 2005; Sivasundar and Hey, 2005; Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genetic studies.

claim: C. elegans has a mode of reproduction called androdioecy.
source: C. elegans has a very peculiar mode of reproduction called androdioecy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans reproduction.

claim: C. elegans can reproduce either by self-fertilizing (selfing) hermaphrodites or by hermaphrodites (XX) breeding with males (X0).
source: It can reproduce either by self-fertilizing (selfing) hermaphrodites or by hermaphrodites (XX) breeding with males (X0).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans reproduction.

claim: C. elegans hermaphrodites develop a female soma, and early in adulthood produce sperm in limited quantities (ca. 200–300 sperm cells).
source: Hermaphrodites develop a female soma, and early in adulthood produce sperm in limited quantities (ca. 200–300 sperm cells).
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans hermaphrodite development.

claim: Males occur by non-disjunction of the X chromosomes at meiosis or in the progeny of male-hermaphrodite crosses.
source: Males occur by non-disjunction of the X chromosomes at meiosis or in the progeny of male-hermaphrodite crosses.
evidence: This is established knowledge about male generation in C. elegans.

claim: The non-disjunction of X chromosomes occurs overall at a low frequency (e.g., 0.1%) in the laboratory, and this frequency varies with genotype and the environment.
source: The non-disjunction of X chromosomes occurs overall at a low frequency (e.g., 0.1%) in the laboratory, and this frequency varies with genotype and the environment (Hodgkin and Doniach, 1997; Teotonio et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to laboratory studies.

claim: In natural populations, outcrossing does occur but the overall proportion of males is low, generally similar to the estimated rate of chromosomal non-disjunction measured in the lab.
source: In natural populations, outcrossing does occur but the overall proportion of males is low, generally similar to the estimated rate of chromosomal non-disjunction measured in the lab (Barrière and Félix, 2007; Cutter et al., 2009; Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009; Andersen et al., 2012; Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to field studies.

claim: In rare instances, outcrossing is evident from a high proportion of males or of heterozygotes in a given sample.
source: In rare instances, outcrossing is evident from a high proportion of males or of heterozygotes in a given sample (Sivasundar and Hey, 2005; Barrière and Félix, 2007; Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to field studies.

claim: The combination of metapopulation dynamics, a very low outcrossing rate and selection has a major impact on the C. elegans genome.
source: This combination of metapopulation dynamics, a very low outcrossing rate and selection has a major impact on the C. elegans genome (Barrière and Félix, 2005b, 2007; Cutter, 2006; Cutter et al., 2009; Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009; Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genetic studies.

claim: Metapopulation dynamics, low outcrossing rate and selection reduce the effective population size, and thus genetic diversity, and can wipe out diversity in a large genomic region.
source: These three factors reduce the effective population size, and thus genetic diversity, and can wipe out diversity in a large genomic region.
evidence: This is an inference from population genetic theory and data.

claim: Positively selected alleles carry with them a large part of the genome by linkage, at the scale of megabases, particularly in the center of chromosomes where recombination is low.
source: Indeed, positively selected alleles carry with them a large part of the genome by linkage, at the scale of megabases, particularly in the center of chromosomes where recombination is low.
evidence: This is an inference from population genetic theory and data.

claim: Most C. elegans isolates carry a recently swept genotype spanning a large part of chromosome V.
source: For example, most C. elegans isolates carry a recently swept genotype spanning a large part of chromosome V; several other chromosomes have also experienced detectable sweeps (Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andersen et al., 2012.

claim: Several other chromosomes have also experienced detectable sweeps.
source: For example, most C. elegans isolates carry a recently swept genotype spanning a large part of chromosome V; several other chromosomes have also experienced detectable sweeps (Andersen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andersen et al., 2012.

claim: Because of high linkage disequilibrium due to selfing, selective sweeps may cover large fractions of chromosomes and have erased much genetic diversity.
source: Because of high linkage disequilibrium due to selfing, selective sweeps may cover large fractions of chromosomes and have erased much genetic diversity.
evidence: This is an inference from population genetic theory and data.

claim: Background selection may further reduce linked genetic diversity in C. elegans.
source: Background selection (the loss of non-deleterious variants due to selection against linked deleterious alleles) may further reduce linked genetic diversity in this selfing species (Rockman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rockman et al., 2010.

claim: Genome-wide pairwise genetic diversity in C. elegans is low (ca. 10^-3/bp), especially compared to outcrossing relatives.
source: As a consequence, genome-wide pairwise genetic diversity is low (ca. 10−3/bp), especially compared to outcrossing relatives (Jovelin et al., 2003; Cutter et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2010; Dey et al., 2013; Gimond et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genetic studies.

claim: Much of the C. elegans genome has been shaped by selection at linked sites, not directly by selection at the locus of interest.
source: Overall, this means that much of the C. elegans genome has been shaped by selection at linked sites, not directly by selection at the locus of interest.
evidence: This is an inference from population genetic data.

claim: Recent events in historical times, perhaps mediated by humans, may have had a significant impact on C. elegans.
source: These extreme sweeps also mean that recent events in historical times, perhaps mediated by humans, may have had a significant impact on C. elegans.
evidence: This is speculation based on genetic patterns.

claim: Most animal species that reproduce by outcrossing suffer from inbreeding depression through the accumulation of deleterious recessive alleles.
source: Most animal species that reproduce by outcrossing suffer from inbreeding depression through the accumulation of deleterious recessive alleles.
evidence: This is established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: In a predominantly self-fertilizing organism, such as C. elegans, alleles are most often in a homozygous state due to repeated selfing, which allows deleterious recessive alleles to be purged by natural selection.
source: In a predominantly self-fertilizing organism, such as C. elegans, alleles are most often in a homozygous state due to repeated selfing, which allows deleterious recessive alleles to be purged by natural selection.
evidence: This is an inference from population genetic theory.

claim: Wild C. elegans suffer from outbreeding depression instead of inbreeding depression.
source: Instead of inbreeding depression, wild C. elegans suffer from outbreeding depression (Dolgin et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dolgin et al., 2007.

claim: Outbreeding depression in C. elegans is best explained by the fact that selfing creates and maintains beneficial gene combinations, while outcrossing favors their disruption.
source: This phenomenon is best explained by the fact that selfing creates and maintains beneficial gene combinations, while outcrossing favors their disruption.
evidence: This is an inference from experimental data.

claim: The progeny of outcrossing are less fit than are the progeny of selfing in C. elegans.
source: Thus, the progeny of outcrossing are less fit than are the progeny of selfing.
evidence: This is an inference from outbreeding depression data.

claim: Under certain circumstances of experimental evolution, outbreeding may contribute positively to C. elegans adaptation and inbreeding depression may reappear.
source: However, at least under certain circumstances of experimental evolution, outbreeding may contribute positively to C. elegans adaptation and inbreeding depression may reappear (Morran et al., 2009; Teotonio et al., 2012; Carvalho et al., 2014; Chelo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental evolution studies.

claim: C. elegans possesses a widespread genetic incompatibility system, whereby a sperm poison (PEEL-1) arrests the development of embryos that do not synthesize the antidote (ZEEL-1).
source: Contributing also to a reduction in effective outcrossing, C. elegans possesses a widespread genetic incompatibility system, whereby a sperm poison (PEEL-1) arrests the development of embryos that do not synthesize the antidote (ZEEL-1) (Seidel et al., 2008, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Seidel et al., 2008, 2011.

claim: The zeel-1 and peel-1 genes are closely linked on chromosome I.
source: The zeel-1 and peel-1 genes are closely linked on chromosome I.
evidence: This is established knowledge from genetic studies.

claim: The two allelic combinations of zeel-1 and peel-1, with both genes or without both genes, co-exist in the same geographical location, and the rest of the genome shows evidence of mixing.
source: The two allelic combinations, with both genes or without both genes, co-exist in the same geographical location, and the rest of the genome shows evidence of mixing.
evidence: This is supported by genetic data.

claim: The PEEL-1/ZEEL-1 incompatibility system may contribute to lowering the effective outcrossing rate.
source: Yet this system, and other incompatibilities, may further contribute to lowering the effective outcrossing rate.
evidence: This is speculation based on the nature of the incompatibility system.

claim: C. elegans has evolved selfing from an ancestor that reproduced through females and males.
source: C. elegans has evolved selfing from an ancestor that reproduced through females and males (see Box 2).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic inference.

claim: Male-specific genes in C. elegans are overall conserved yet appear to be subject to relaxed selection.
source: Male-specific genes are overall conserved yet appear to be subject to relaxed selection (Cutter, 2008; Thomas et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claim: C. elegans males still sense female pheromones from closely related species.
source: Although C. elegans males still sense female pheromones from closely related species, hermaphrodites no longer produce pheromones to attract males (Chasnov and Chow, 2002; Chasnov et al., 2007), suggesting a partial degeneration of hermaphrodite outcrossing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: C. elegans hermaphrodites no longer produce pheromones to attract males.
source: Although C. elegans males still sense female pheromones from closely related species, hermaphrodites no longer produce pheromones to attract males (Chasnov and Chow, 2002; Chasnov et al., 2007), suggesting a partial degeneration of hermaphrodite outcrossing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: The loss of pheromone production in hermaphrodites suggests a partial degeneration of hermaphrodite outcrossing.
source: Although C. elegans males still sense female pheromones from closely related species, hermaphrodites no longer produce pheromones to attract males (Chasnov and Chow, 2002; Chasnov et al., 2007), suggesting a partial degeneration of hermaphrodite outcrossing.
evidence: This is an inference from behavioral data.

claim: Some aspects of mating behavior in C. elegans males appear to have degenerated, such as the ability to deposit a copulatory plug.
source: On the male side, some aspects of mating behavior also appear to have degenerated, such as the ability to deposit a copulatory plug (Palopoli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Palopoli et al., 2008.

claim: C. elegans shares its microhabitat with arthropods and with other microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) and invertebrates.
source: C. elegans shares its microhabitat with arthropods and with other microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) and invertebrates (Table 1), including other nematodes such as Oscheius, Pristionchus, Panagrellus and other Caenorhabditis species, such as Caenorhabditis briggsae (Kiontke et al., 2011; Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and observational data.

claim: C. elegans shares its microhabitat with other nematodes such as Oscheius, Pristionchus, Panagrellus and other Caenorhabditis species, such as Caenorhabditis briggsae.
source: C. elegans shares its microhabitat with arthropods and with other microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) and invertebrates (Table 1), including other nematodes such as Oscheius, Pristionchus, Panagrellus and other Caenorhabditis species, such as Caenorhabditis briggsae (Kiontke et al., 2011; Félix and Duveau, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to field studies.

claim: C. elegans shares its rotting fruit habitat with two other top model organisms, Drosophila melanogaster and Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: If not with E. coli, it is noteworthy that C. elegans shares its rotting fruit habitat with two other top model organisms, Drosophila melanogaster and Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Fay and Benavides, 2005; Diezmann and Dietrich, 2009; Schacherer et al., 2009; Charron et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A specific association is found between another Caenorhabditis species (C. drosophilae) and another Drosophila species: this nematode species feeds on rotting cactus in desert areas and its dauer juveniles use a local Drosophila species as a vector to move between cacti.
source: A specific association is actually found between another Caenorhabditis species and another Drosophila species: this nematode species, C. drosophilae, feeds on rotting cactus in desert areas and its dauer juveniles use a local Drosophila species as a vector to move between cacti (Kiontke, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kiontke, 1997.

claim: The C. elegans diet mainly consists of bacteria and small eukaryotes.
source: The C. elegans diet mainly consists of bacteria and small eukaryotes (Félix and Braendle, 2010; Félix and Duveau, 2012), but has not been further characterized.
evidence: This is supported by citations to field studies.

claim: As C. elegans adults grow old, they can serve as food to the same microorganisms.
source: The trophic interaction between the nematode and its prey is not univocal: as C. elegans adults grow old, they can serve as food to the same microorganisms.
evidence: This is an observation from field or laboratory studies.

claim: From co-occurrence in the wild and from laboratory experiments, possible natural predators of C. elegans include small arthropods, such as mites or springtails, other nematodes, such as Pristionchus spp., and trapping nematophagous fungi.
source: From co-occurrence in the wild and from laboratory experiments, possible natural predators include small arthropods, such as mites or springtails (Figure 2H), other nematodes, such as Pristionchus spp., and trapping nematophagous fungi (Lee and Widden, 1996; Kiontke and Sudhaus, 2006; Bento et al., 2010; Maguire et al., 2011; Félix and Duveau, 2012) (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations and observational data.

claim: C. elegans constantly interacts with a variety of obligate and non-obligate parasites, such as fungi, microsporidia, bacteria and viruses.
source: C. elegans also constantly interacts with a variety of obligate and non-obligate parasites, such as fungi, microsporidia, bacteria and viruses (Troemel et al., 2008; Félix et al., 2011; Félix and Duveau, 2012; Hodgkin et al., 2013) (Table 1).

claim: Parasites infect C. elegans via the two most exposed parts of the nematode, the cuticle and the intestine.

claim: Some non-invasive bacteria form a biofilm along the nematode's cuticle or directly stick to it.

claim: Other bacteria proliferate in the nematode gut, which may induce constipation and likely impairs nutrient uptake.
source: Other bacteria proliferate in the nematode gut, which may induce constipation and likely impairs nutrient uptake (Félix and Duveau, 2012).

claim: Some parasites pierce the cuticle (e.g., Drechmeria coniospora).
source: Some pierce the cuticle (e.g., Drechmeria coniospora [Couillault et al., 2004], Figure 2J), while others enter intestinal cells via the apical membrane (e.g., microsporidia and Orsay virus [Troemel et al., 2008; Félix et al., 2011]).

claim: Some parasites enter intestinal cells via the apical membrane (e.g., microsporidia and Orsay virus).
source: Some pierce the cuticle (e.g., Drechmeria coniospora [Couillault et al., 2004], Figure 2J), while others enter intestinal cells via the apical membrane (e.g., microsporidia and Orsay virus [Troemel et al., 2008; Félix et al., 2011]).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: C. elegans rapidly proliferates in the wild upon encountering a food source.
source: First, like other model organisms, C. elegans rapidly proliferates in the wild upon encountering a food source, and can remain in a resting stage for long periods of time.
evidence: This is supported by observational data.

claim: C. elegans can remain in a resting stage for long periods of time.
source: First, like other model organisms, C. elegans rapidly proliferates in the wild upon encountering a food source, and can remain in a resting stage for long periods of time.

claim: C. elegans displays a short generation time compared with many other nematodes.
source: Indeed, C. elegans displays a short generation time compared with many other nematodes and can simply be maintained on cholesterol-supplemented agar plates and fed E. coli.

claim: C. elegans can simply be maintained on cholesterol-supplemented agar plates and fed E. coli.
source: Indeed, C. elegans displays a short generation time compared with many other nematodes and can simply be maintained on cholesterol-supplemented agar plates and fed E. coli.

claim: The natural ability of dauer larvae to live for several months offers a convenient option for short-term storage.

claim: C. elegans survives freezing, which enables their long-term storage at −80°C or in liquid nitrogen.
source: C. elegans survives freezing, which enables their long-term storage at −80°C or in liquid nitrogen—an extremely useful feature for genotype storage and experimental design.

claim: Selfing permits the generation of homozygous stocks, without inbreeding depression.
source: Selfing permits the generation of homozygous stocks, without inbreeding depression.

claim: The ability to induce males makes genetic crosses easy in C. elegans.
source: The ability to induce males makes genetic crosses easy.

claim: C. elegans egg shells are naturally resistant to many environmental stresses, allowing the use of bleach.
source: Third, C. elegans egg shells are naturally resistant to many environmental stresses, allowing the use of bleach.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans egg shell properties.

claim: Bleaching is widely employed in the laboratory: in a population, only embryos will survive bleaching, thus allowing synchronization and removal of microbial contaminants.
source: Bleaching is widely employed in the laboratory: in a population, only embryos will survive bleaching, thus allowing synchronization and removal of microbial contaminants.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans laboratory practice.

claim: A convenient feature of the reference C. elegans strain, N2, that is found in some but not all C. elegans wild isolates or Caenorhabditis species is an active RNA interference pathway.
source: Finally, a convenient feature of the reference C. elegans strain, N2, that is found in some but not all C. elegans wild isolates or Caenorhabditis species is an active RNA interference pathway.

claim: The RNA interference pathway in C. elegans was perhaps selected in response to encounters with viruses and transposons.
source: This pathway was perhaps selected in response to encounters with viruses and transposons (Tijsterman et al., 2002; Félix, 2008; Félix et al., 2011).

claim: For a top model organism such as C. elegans, a large proportion of its genes are, as yet, not associated with any mutant phenotype.

claim: A ubiquitin-mediated response was shown to take part in the C. elegans defense against two wild parasites, Nematocida parisii (microsporidia) and the Orsay virus.
source: Recently, a ubiquitin-mediated response was indeed shown to take part in the C. elegans defense against two wild parasites, Nematocida parisii (microsporidia) and the Orsay virus (Bakowski et al., 2014), as well as in behavioral avoidance of a bacterial pathogen (Chang et al., 2011).

claim: A ubiquitin-mediated response takes part in behavioral avoidance of a bacterial pathogen in C. elegans.

claim: Most Caenorhabditis species reproduce through males and females.

claim: C. elegans, C. briggsae and Caenorhabditis tropicalis are exceptions by having evolved spermatogenesis in a female soma.
